lessons.title: Growth and Developmental Milestones
body: Pediatrics is the medicine of change. A child is not a small adult: physiology, disease patterns and the very definition of normal move with age. Two frameworks organise the work, growth (a quantitative change in size) and development (acquisition of skills across domains).

Growth is tracked on percentile charts. In the United States, the CDC charts are used from age 2 years, and the WHO growth standards, which describe how breastfed infants grow under optimal conditions, are recommended from birth to 2 years. Weight, length (or height) and head circumference are plotted at each visit, and body mass index from age 2. The trajectory matters more than any single point. Crossing two major percentile lines downward, or a weight far below the length percentile, suggests failure to thrive. Most cases come from inadequate caloric intake rather than organic disease. A child with a small head who is otherwise well and tracking along a curve is usually a familial pattern, while a head circumference that accelerates across percentiles raises concern for hydrocephalus or a mass. Newborns lose up to roughly 10 percent of birth weight in the first days and regain it by about two weeks.

Development is divided into gross motor, fine motor, language and social-emotional domains. The sequence is predictable and the timing varies within a range. Approximate anchors: a social smile by about 2 months, head control and rolling in the first half-year, sitting without support at about 6 months, a pincer grasp near 9 to 12 months, walking around 12 months, single words at about 12 months, two-word phrases by 2 years, and a three-word sentence and a child who can be understood by strangers about three-quarters of the time by 3 years. Primitive reflexes, such as the Moro and palmar grasp, should fade over the first months; persistence beyond that suggests a central nervous system problem. Loss of previously acquired skills, called regression, is more worrisome than a simple delay and calls for prompt evaluation.

Surveillance is continuous and informal at every visit, using parent concerns and observation. Formal standardised screening is recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (2020 clinical report) at 9, 18 and 30 months for general development, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months. Tools include the Ages and Stages Questionnaire and the M-CHAT-R/F. A positive screen should lead to referral for diagnostic evaluation and early intervention, and should not be met with waiting to see. Hearing and vision must be checked in any child with speech delay, because uncorrected hearing loss is a common and treatable cause.

A worked example: a 15-month-old is brought in because he is not yet walking. He cruises along furniture, babbles, says two words with meaning, points to what he wants and plays peekaboo. This is within normal limits, since walking independently is expected by about 15 to 18 months. By contrast, a 15-month-old who says no words, does not point, does not respond to his name and has stopped using gestures he once used deserves audiology and autism evaluation. The distinction is isolated variation versus global or domain-wide delay and regression.

lessons.title: Newborn Care and Screening
body: The first minutes of extrauterine life are the greatest physiologic transition a person makes. The lungs must clear fluid and expand, pulmonary vascular resistance falls, and the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus close. The Apgar score, assigned at 1 and 5 minutes, rates colour, heart rate, reflex irritability, tone and respiratory effort from 0 to 2 each. It describes the infant's condition and the response to resuscitation. It does not decide whether to start resuscitation, which is guided by breathing, heart rate and tone, and it does not predict long-term outcome on its own.

Routine newborn care includes thermoregulation with skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding support, vitamin K to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding (newborns have low stores, sterile guts and immature clotting factor synthesis), and antibiotic eye prophylaxis against gonococcal ophthalmia. Hepatitis B vaccination timing is discussed in the immunization lesson. A thorough examination looks for congenital anomalies, hip instability with the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres, a red reflex in each eye (absent or white reflex suggests cataract, retinoblastoma or other pathology), femoral pulses, and cleft palate.

Universal screening catches treatable disease before symptoms. Dried blood spot screening covers dozens of conditions, with the exact panel set by each state, including phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and others. Hearing screening is done before discharge. Critical congenital heart disease screening uses pulse oximetry at 24 hours or later, and in the AAP algorithm a saturation below 90 percent at either site is an immediate fail that triggers echocardiography. A pass needs 95 percent or more in both the right hand and a foot, with a difference of no more than 3 percentage points; borderline results are retested once, and a persistent borderline or differential result also fails (AAP clinical report, 2025).

Jaundice is visible in most newborns. Physiologic jaundice appears after the first 24 hours, peaks at about day 3 to 5 in term infants and resolves in one to two weeks. It happens because fetal red cells are short-lived, hepatic glucuronyl transferase activity is immature and enterohepatic recirculation is increased. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathologic and suggests haemolysis such as ABO or Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency or hereditary spherocytosis. The Coombs test identifies immune haemolysis. Breastfeeding jaundice reflects poor intake and dehydration in the first week; breast milk jaundice arises later and peaks near the second week in a thriving infant. Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiologic and points to biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis or metabolic disease; persistent jaundice with pale stools beyond about 2 weeks demands fractionated bilirubin.

Unconjugated bilirubin is neurotoxic. At very high levels it crosses the immature blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia, causing acute bilirubin encephalopathy and then kernicterus, with athetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss and gaze palsy. The AAP 2022 guideline uses hour-specific bilirubin thresholds that depend on gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors to decide on phototherapy and exchange transfusion. Phototherapy converts bilirubin to water-soluble isomers excreted without conjugation. The approach is to measure, plot, treat according to the threshold and arrange follow-up, and not to rely on visual estimation alone.

lessons.title: Common Neonatal Problems
body: A distressed newborn presents with a limited vocabulary of signs: tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, cyanosis, poor feeding, lethargy or temperature instability. The skill is matching the gestational age, the timing and the context to the cause.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is the disease of surfactant deficiency in preterm infants. Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant late in gestation, and without it surface tension collapses the alveoli, so atelectasis, hypoxia and a stiff lung follow. The chest radiograph shows a ground-glass, reticulogranular pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Antenatal corticosteroids given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery accelerate lung maturity. Treatment is respiratory support and exogenous surfactant. Complications include bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, intraventricular haemorrhage and patent ductus arteriosus. By contrast, transient tachypnoea of the newborn is a self-limited condition of retained lung fluid seen in term infants delivered by caesarean section, with perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures, resolving within a few days. Meconium aspiration affects post-term infants with meconium-stained fluid and shows patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn produces profound hypoxaemia out of proportion to the radiograph.

Early-onset sepsis presents in the first 72 hours, usually from organisms acquired from the maternal genital tract, namely group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria. Late-onset sepsis, after the first week, reflects postnatal and hospital acquisition. Signs are subtle and nonspecific, so low thresholds for blood culture and empirical antibiotics apply, and lumbar puncture is considered when meningitis is possible. Maternal screening for group B Streptococcus at 36 to 37 weeks, with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for carriers and other risk situations, reduced early-onset disease (AAP 2019 report). Risk is higher with prematurity, prolonged rupture of membranes and maternal chorioamnionitis.

Hypoglycaemia is common in infants of diabetic mothers (fetal hyperinsulinism), those who are small or large for gestational age, and preterm infants. Because the brain depends on glucose, symptomatic hypoglycaemia (jitteriness, seizures, lethargy) is treated urgently with glucose. Infants of diabetic mothers also have macrosomia, polycythaemia and hypocalcaemia, and an increased risk of congenital heart disease and caudal regression.

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is bowel necrosis in preterm infants after enteral feeding starts. The mucosa is immature, blood flow is labile and the microbiome is abnormal. Presentation includes feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stools. The abdominal radiograph shows pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall) and, in perforation, free air. Treatment is bowel rest, antibiotics, decompression, and surgery for perforation or necrosis. Human milk is protective.

Birth injuries include caput succedaneum (crosses suture lines), cephalohaematoma (does not cross sutures and may calcify), clavicle fracture and brachial plexus palsy. Erb palsy involves C5 and C6 with the arm adducted and internally rotated, while the grasp is preserved.

lessons.title: Chromosomal Disorders
body: Chromosomal disorders arise from abnormal chromosome number (aneuploidy) or structure, and usually from errors in meiosis, so risk rises with maternal age for trisomies. The clinical logic is pattern recognition: a recognisable face, a typical set of organ anomalies and a predictable developmental course, confirmed by karyotype, microarray or targeted testing.

Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. Most cases are nondisjunction in maternal meiosis, about 4 percent are Robertsonian translocations, which carry a recurrence risk for the parents, and a few are mosaic. Newborns are hypotonic with upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile, a single palmar crease, a wide gap between the first and second toes and brachycephaly. Associated problems include atrioventricular septal defect (the characteristic heart lesion, so echocardiography is advised in every newborn), duodenal atresia (the double bubble sign), Hirschsprung disease, congenital hypothyroidism and later acquired hypothyroidism, hearing loss, celiac disease, atlantoaxial instability, leukaemia including a transient myeloproliferative state in newborns, and early-onset Alzheimer disease. The AAP health supervision report (2022) organises the screening schedule for these conditions.

Trisomy 18 (Edwards) has clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, a small jaw, and heart defects. Trisomy 13 (Patau) shows holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly and cutis aplasia. Both carry high infant mortality.

Turner syndrome (45,X) affects girls. Features are short stature, a webbed neck, a shield chest with widely spaced nipples, lymphoedema of the hands and feet in the newborn, and streak gonads leading to primary amenorrhoea and absent puberty with elevated FSH. Cardiac associations are bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, and renal anomalies such as horseshoe kidney occur. Intelligence is typically normal. Growth hormone and oestrogen replacement are used. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) affects boys who are tall with long limbs, small firm testes, gynaecomastia and infertility from azoospermia, with low testosterone and high FSH and LH. It is often diagnosed late and learning and language difficulties are common.

Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. It is an X-linked disorder caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 with hypermethylation and silencing of the gene. The phenotype includes a long face, large ears, macro-orchidism after puberty, autism features and hyperextensible joints. Anticipation is seen because the repeat expands when transmitted through a female carrier. Premutation carriers can develop fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome or primary ovarian insufficiency.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge and velocardiofacial) results from a microdeletion, and is remembered with CATCH-22: cardiac anomalies (conotruncal defects such as tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus), abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia with T-cell deficiency, cleft palate, and hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism. The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail to develop. Confirmation uses chromosomal microarray or FISH. Live vaccines are withheld if T-cell function is severely reduced. A newborn with a conotruncal defect and seizures from low calcium is the classic stem, and calcium and immune function must be checked.

Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes are imprinting disorders of the 15q11-13 region, depending on which parental copy is lost: loss of paternal genes causes Prader-Willi (hypotonia, then hyperphagia and obesity), and loss of maternal genes causes Angelman (happy demeanour, ataxia, seizures, absent speech).

lessons.title: Inherited Metabolic and Single-Gene Diseases
body: Inborn errors of metabolism are single-gene defects in an enzyme or transporter. Most are autosomal recessive, so consider consanguinity or a family history of unexplained infant deaths. A previously well newborn who becomes lethargic, feeds poorly, vomits, develops tachypnoea and seizures after days of normal feeding should prompt suspicion, because the toxic precursor accumulates only once protein or sugar feeds begin. First-line studies are glucose, blood gas, ammonia, lactate, ketones and urine reducing substances.

Phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase (or tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor). Phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine becomes essential, so untreated children develop intellectual disability, seizures, fair skin and hair from reduced melanin, eczema and a musty or mousy odour. Newborn screening finds it before damage, and treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet begun early. Maternal PKU is a teratogenic risk, so affected women need dietary control before and during pregnancy. Galactosemia, from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, presents after milk feeds with jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, vomiting and bilateral cataracts, and there is a predisposition to Escherichia coli sepsis. Reducing substances are positive in the urine, and the treatment is removing galactose (lactose) from the diet, using soy or elemental formula.

Urea cycle disorders, such as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which is X-linked, cause hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis, lethargy and vomiting, with normal glucose and no acidosis in the early phase. Organic acidaemias cause anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis. Fatty acid oxidation defects such as medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness, so treatment is avoiding fasting.

Lysosomal storage diseases have progressive course with coarse features, organomegaly or neurodegeneration. Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) gives a cherry-red macula and an exaggerated startle with regression but no organomegaly, whereas Gaucher and Niemann-Pick disease have hepatosplenomegaly.

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease of the CFTR chloride channel, with F508del the most common variant. Defective chloride and bicarbonate secretion yields thick secretions in the lungs, pancreas, gut and sweat glands. Presentation includes meconium ileus in the newborn, recurrent pneumonia with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, steatorrhoea with failure to thrive from pancreatic insufficiency and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, nasal polyps and rectal prolapse. Males have congenital absence of the vas deferens. Most US cases are detected by newborn screening for immunoreactive trypsinogen, then confirmed with a sweat chloride test, where a value of 60 mmol/L or more is diagnostic. CFTR modulator therapies, which improve channel function, have transformed outcomes for many variants.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive, caused by out-of-frame deletions in the dystrophin gene. Boys present at 3 to 5 years with delayed walking, difficulty rising from the floor (Gowers sign), calf pseudohypertrophy and elevated creatine kinase. Becker dystrophy has in-frame mutations and a milder course. Spinal muscular atrophy, from SMN1 deletion, causes a floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and is now on many newborn screening panels because gene-based therapy works best early.

lessons.title: Congenital Infections and Structural Anomalies
body: A congenital infection is one acquired in utero. The classic acronym TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents including syphilis, varicella and Zika, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex) groups them because they share presentations: growth restriction, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, rash or petechiae, and abnormal eyes. The timing of infection in pregnancy, not only the organism, determines severity; earlier infection generally causes worse structural damage.

Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection in developed countries. Most infants are asymptomatic, but sensorineural hearing loss may develop later and is the main long-term morbidity. Symptomatic infants have periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis and a blueberry-muffin rash. Congenital toxoplasmosis, acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat, gives chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Congenital rubella presents with cataracts, sensorineural deafness and patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis, and has become rare where vaccination is universal. Congenital syphilis causes hepatosplenomegaly, snuffles, a desquamating rash on the palms and soles, and periosteal changes, with Hutchinson teeth and saddle nose appearing later if untreated; penicillin is the treatment and maternal screening in pregnancy is the prevention. Neonatal herpes can be disseminated, localised to skin, eye and mouth, or encephalitic, and often follows delivery through an infected genital tract, so primary maternal infection near term carries the highest risk. Congenital Zika infection causes microcephaly with brain calcifications. Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal hydrops.

Neural tube defects result from failure of closure of the neural tube in the first month. Folate deficiency is the major modifiable risk factor, and supplementation before conception reduces risk. Spina bifida occulta is often asymptomatic, with a tuft of hair or a dimple over the lumbar spine. Meningocele and myelomeningocele contain a sac with meninges, and the latter contains neural tissue, with lower limb weakness and neurogenic bladder. The Arnold-Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus are linked with myelomeningocele. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein is raised in open neural tube defects. Anencephaly is incompatible with life.

Developmental dysplasia of the hip comprises instability to frank dislocation. Risk factors are female sex, breech presentation, family history and oligohydramnios. The Ortolani manoeuvre reduces a dislocated hip with a clunk and Barlow provokes dislocation of an unstable hip. After about 3 months these signs fade, and limited abduction and a leg-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign) appear. Ultrasound is the imaging study before 4 to 6 months, then radiography. Treatment in young infants is a Pavlik harness.

Abdominal wall defects: gastroschisis is a defect lateral to the umbilicus with no covering sac, bowel exposed to amniotic fluid, and few associated anomalies. Omphalocele is a midline defect covered by a membranous sac and is associated with other anomalies and chromosomal disorders such as trisomy 18 and with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Cleft lip and palate require feeding support, surgery and monitoring for otitis media and speech.

lessons.title: Immunization Principles and Schedules
body: Vaccines teach the immune system to recognise a pathogen without causing the disease. Live attenuated vaccines (measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, rotavirus, intranasal influenza, oral polio historically) replicate weakly and produce durable immunity, but are generally avoided in pregnancy and in severe immunodeficiency. Inactivated, subunit, conjugate, toxoid and mRNA vaccines cannot replicate and are safe in immunocompromised hosts, though responses may be weaker and need boosters. Conjugate vaccines link a polysaccharide capsule to a carrier protein, converting a T-independent antigen into a T-dependent one so that infants respond and memory forms; this is why Haemophilus influenzae type b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines work under age 2, whereas plain polysaccharide vaccines do not.

In the United States the schedule is issued by the CDC on the advice of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), and published jointly with professional organisations including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians. The AAP publishes its own schedule too. This area is moving fast, so the dated facts as of October 2026 are these. On 5 January 2026 the CDC, without a vote of ACIP, issued a revised schedule that kept routine recommendations for 11 diseases (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal, polio, measles, mumps, rubella, HPV and varicella) and moved rotavirus, influenza, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, RSV, COVID-19 and meningococcal ACWY to high-risk or shared clinical decision-making. On 26 January 2026 the AAP published its own 2026 schedule, endorsed by 12 organisations, which keeps routine recommendations for 18 diseases. On 16 March 2026 a federal court (AAP v. Kennedy) stayed the January CDC memo, the appointments of the reconstituted ACIP and its votes, which restored the June 2024 schedule. HHS appealed, and the First Circuit was scheduled to hear argument on 6 October 2026, so the legal status may change. A clinician should check the current published CDC and AAP schedules for exact ages and intervals and not rely on memory. The traditional schedule that the AAP continues to

recommend is as follows. Hepatitis B vaccine begins in infancy. Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, inactivated poliovirus, pneumococcal conjugate and rotavirus vaccines begin at 2 months. Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella are first given at 12 to 15 months with a second dose at 4 to 6 years. Hepatitis A is given from 12 months. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended from 6 months. Tdap is given in early adolescence, and the HPV and meningococcal vaccines are given in adolescence. Catch-up schedules exist for children who are behind, and an interrupted series is continued, not restarted.

True contraindications are few: a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or a component, and for live vaccines severe immunodeficiency and pregnancy. Rotavirus vaccine is avoided with a history of intussusception or severe combined immunodeficiency. Pertussis-containing vaccines are avoided if encephalopathy occurred within 7 days of a prior dose. Precautions, such as moderate or severe acute illness, call for judgement. Mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotic use, prematurity and breastfeeding are not contraindications. Egg allergy is no longer a barrier to influenza vaccination in most circumstances.

Monitoring safety is a layered system. Clinical trials come first, then post-licensure surveillance through the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (a hypothesis-generating passive system), the Vaccine Safety Datalink and others. Large studies have found no link between MMR vaccine and autism; the original 1998 paper claiming one was retracted. Real, rare risks do exist, such as febrile seizures after MMR in a small proportion, and intussusception with a prior rotavirus vaccine, and clinicians should name them honestly in counselling.

Vaccine hesitancy is best met with a presumptive, respectful recommendation, open questions to find the specific concern, and a clear statement of the evidence. State exemption and school-entry laws vary by state. Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated, but its threshold is high for highly contagious diseases such as measles (roughly 95 percent coverage is needed).

A worked example: a 4-month-old arrives 2 months late for the second set of vaccines, with a mild cold and no fever. The correct approach is to give the due vaccines now and continue the series without restarting, since a mild illness is not a contraindication and delay only prolongs vulnerability.

lessons.title: Fever and Serious Bacterial Infection
body: Fever is a symptom, and the challenge in a young child is separating the usual viral illness from the small proportion with serious bacterial infection (bacteraemia, meningitis, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, bone and joint infection). The younger the infant the less reliable the examination, the more immature the immune response, and the lower the threshold for a full workup.

Infants in the first month with a rectal temperature of at least 38.0 C (100.4 F) are managed as an emergency, and the youngest get the most aggressive workup. Under the AAP 2021 guideline, a well-appearing infant 8 to 21 days old gets blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid studies, empirical intravenous antibiotics and admission. At 22 to 28 days the approach is stratified by urinalysis and inflammatory markers: with abnormal markers, lumbar puncture, antibiotics and admission; with normal markers and urinalysis, lumbar puncture and antibiotics become optional, and the infant may be observed in hospital off antibiotics or, after a normal cerebrospinal fluid result, at home after an antibiotic dose if reliable 24-hour follow-up exists. Infants under 8 days and ill-appearing infants of any age fall outside that algorithm and receive a full workup and admission. The pathogens are group B Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes and herpes simplex virus, so acyclovir is added when herpes is suspected, for example with vesicles, seizures or a maternal history. For well-appearing infants 29 to 60 days, and as above for 22 to 28 days, the AAP 2021 guideline offers a stepwise approach using urinalysis, absolute neutrophil count, C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, with age-based decisions about lumbar puncture, antibiotics and admission or observation. Older children
are risk-stratified clinically, and since pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate vaccination, occult bacteraemia has become uncommon in vaccinated children.

Bacterial meningitis outside the neonatal period is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, with the decline of Haemophilus influenzae type b after vaccination. Features include fever, headache, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness, a bulging fontanelle in infants and, with meningococcus, a petechial or purpuric rash that can progress to purpura fulminans. Cerebrospinal fluid shows high neutrophils, high protein and low glucose, in contrast with viral meningitis, which shows lymphocytes with normal glucose and mildly raised protein. Treatment must not wait for lumbar puncture when the child is unstable or imaging is needed: take blood cultures, start empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone as the evidence supports, since steroids reduce hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae meningitis. Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common sequela, so audiology is done on recovery. Household contacts of meningococcal disease receive chemoprophylaxis.

Urinary tract infection is the most common serious bacterial infection in febrile infants. Escherichia coli causes most. Diagnosis requires pyuria or a positive urinalysis plus growth of a uropathogen at a significant count from a catheterised or clean specimen. A bag specimen is unreliable and only useful if negative. Febrile UTI in young children is treated with antibiotics, and renal and bladder ultrasound is recommended after the first febrile UTI. A voiding cystourethrogram is considered for abnormal ultrasound or recurrence, to look for vesicoureteral reflux, which predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal scarring.

Osteomyelitis and septic arthritis present with fever and a limp or refusal to bear weight. Staphylococcus aureus is the dominant organism, and Kingella kingae is notable in young children. Septic arthritis of the hip is an emergency because of damage to the femoral head blood supply; the Kocher criteria (fever, nonweight-bearing, high ESR, and high white cell count) estimate the probability. Joint aspiration or surgical drainage plus antibiotics treat it. Transient synovitis, a viral self-limited cause of hip pain, is a diagnosis of exclusion.

lessons.title: Childhood Rashes and Common Infections
body: Rash with fever is a recurring clinical puzzle. The approach combines the morphology of the rash, its distribution and evolution, the prodrome, and the immunization status.

Measles begins with the three Cs, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, with fever up to 40 C, then Koplik spots (small white spots on the buccal mucosa) and a maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. Complications include otitis media, pneumonia (the most common cause of death), encephalitis and, years later, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Vitamin A is given to children with measles in many settings. The virus is airborne and extremely contagious, and cases cluster where vaccination coverage is low. Rubella causes mild illness with postauricular lymphadenopathy, and its importance is congenital rubella. Roseola (human herpesvirus 6) gives three or four days of high fever followed by a rash as the fever breaks, and the child is often well-appearing and may have a febrile seizure. Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, parvovirus B19) gives slapped-cheek erythema and a lacy rash, and it causes aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease from coxsackievirus presents with oral ulcers and vesicles on the hands and feet. Varicella shows vesicles in successive crops in all stages at once; complications include secondary bacterial skin infection, cerebellitis and pneumonia, and the shingles risk persists. Scarlet fever follows group A Streptococcus pharyngitis, with a sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and Pastia lines. Kawasaki disease is addressed in the cardiac track.

Acute otitis media follows eustachian tube dysfunction, usually after a viral upper respiratory infection, with Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis the main bacteria. Diagnosis requires middle ear effusion with a bulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhoea, along with signs of acute inflammation; effusion alone is otitis media with effusion and does not need antibiotics. The AAP 2013 guideline supports observation without antibiotics in selected older children with mild unilateral disease, and treatment for young children and for severe illness, with amoxicillin as the first-line choice for most. Complications include mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling and protrusion of the ear), tympanic membrane perforation and conductive hearing loss, and persistent effusion with speech delay prompts audiology and consideration of tympanostomy tubes.

Group A streptococcal pharyngitis occurs in school-aged children with sudden sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical nodes and no cough. The IDSA October 2025 partial update recommends using a clinical scoring system, such as Centor or McIsaac, in children aged 3 years and older and adults to decide who needs testing at all, so that low-probability patients are not tested. For those who are tested, the 2012 guideline advice still stands while the remaining sections are updated: a rapid antigen test and, if negative in a child, a backup throat culture confirm the diagnosis. Treatment is penicillin or amoxicillin, mainly to prevent acute rheumatic fever, which follows pharyngitis (not skin infection), and to shorten illness. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis can follow throat or skin infection and is not prevented by antibiotics. Viral pharyngitis, with cough, hoarseness and conjunctivitis, needs no testing for strep. Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis presents with exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes. Amoxicillin given in error causes a rash, and splenic rupture risk calls for avoiding contact sports.

A worked example: a 6-year-old has a 2-day fever, headache and sore throat without cough, and the rapid test is positive. The right choice is a penicillin-class antibiotic, whose main benefit is preventing rheumatic fever, which damages heart valves and was the reason treatment guidelines emphasise the diagnosis.

lessons.title: Pediatric Respiratory Disease
body: Children are prone to respiratory disease because their airways are narrow, resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius reduction, the chest wall is compliant, and viral exposure is constant. Localising the problem by sound and anatomy is the key. Stridor, a harsh inspiratory sound, indicates extrathoracic upper airway obstruction. Wheeze, an expiratory musical sound, indicates intrathoracic lower airway narrowing. Grunting signals alveolar disease.

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is caused most often by parainfluenza virus in children aged 6 months to 3 years. It causes a barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor, worse at night, with the steeple sign (subglottic narrowing) on an anteroposterior neck radiograph, which is not required. A single dose of corticosteroid is the mainstay and nebulised epinephrine is used for stridor at rest. Epiglottitis, once a result of Haemophilus influenzae type b, is now rare after vaccination. It presents with a toxic-appearing child with drooling, muffled voice and a tripod posture, and the thumb sign on a lateral radiograph. The airway must be secured by experienced personnel and the child should not be agitated or examined with a tongue depressor. Bacterial tracheitis follows a viral illness with high fever and a toxic child, usually Staphylococcus aureus.

Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the small airways in infants younger than 2 years, most commonly from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), with a winter peak. Inflammation and sloughed epithelium obstruct the bronchioles, producing tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, retractions and hypoxia after a few days of cold symptoms. It is a clinical diagnosis. The AAP 2014 guideline recommends supportive care: nasal suctioning, hydration and oxygen when saturation is persistently low, and advises against routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, chest radiographs and chest physiotherapy. Prevention uses nirsevimab or clesrovimab (monoclonal antibodies) for infants, and maternal RSV vaccination in late pregnancy has been introduced; consult current recommendations on timing. Apnoea is a particular risk in young infants.

Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Symptoms are recurrent cough, wheeze, chest tightness and dyspnoea, often worse at night and with exercise, viruses or allergens, and often with atopy. Diagnosis combines history and spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility in children old enough to perform it. Severity is classified as intermittent or persistent and treatment stepped by control. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred long-term controller; short-acting beta-agonists relieve symptoms. Current guidance (NHLBI 2007, with updates in 2020, and GINA) has moved to combined anti-inflammatory reliever approaches in some age groups. Exacerbations are treated with bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroids and oxygen, and a child who tires, becomes quiet and has a silent chest is in danger. Education, trigger avoidance and written action plans reduce morbidity.

Pneumonia in children is most commonly viral in the young, and in bacterial cases Streptococcus pneumoniae is the usual pathogen, with Mycoplasma pneumoniae more common in school-aged children and adolescents (walking pneumonia, with an insidious cough and extrapulmonary features). Fever, tachypnoea and focal findings suggest the diagnosis. Amoxicillin is the empirical choice for typical outpatient pneumonia, and complicated cases include parapneumonic effusion and empyema.

Foreign body aspiration occurs in toddlers who put objects in their mouths. Sudden choking followed by cough, wheeze or unilateral hyperinflation (air trapping seen on expiratory or decubitus films) suggests it, and rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia are considered when infections are recurrent.

lessons.title: Pediatric Gastrointestinal Disease
body: Gastrointestinal complaints in children are best organised by age and by whether vomiting is bilious. Bilious vomiting (green) means obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater until proven otherwise and is a surgical emergency in the newborn, because midgut volvulus can strangulate the bowel within hours.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents at 2 to 8 weeks, classically in a firstborn male, with progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeds, a hungry infant, an olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium and visible peristalsis. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and paradoxical aciduria. Ultrasound shows a thickened elongated pylorus. Resuscitation, correcting the electrolytes, comes first, and pyloromyotomy is curative. Malrotation with midgut volvulus presents with bilious vomiting in the first weeks, a rapidly ill child and the corkscrew sign on an upper gastrointestinal contrast study, which is the test of choice in a stable infant; surgical Ladd procedure is required. Intestinal atresias present with bilious vomiting and the double bubble in duodenal atresia. Hirschsprung disease is absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel from failure of neural crest migration. It presents with failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distension and, after rectal examination, an explosive release of stool. It may cause enterocolitis, and is associated with Down syndrome. Contrast enema shows a transition zone and rectal suction biopsy confirms the absence of ganglion cells. Meconium ileus points to cystic fibrosis.

Intussusception is telescoping of bowel, usually ileocolic, in children aged 6 months to 3 years. The child has paroxysmal colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, intervals of lethargy, vomiting, a sausage-shaped mass and currant jelly stools. Ultrasound shows a target sign. Air or contrast enema is diagnostic and therapeutic, and surgery is needed for perforation or failed reduction. A pathologic lead point (Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma) is likelier in older children. Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the vitelline duct, follows the rule of 2s and causes painless rectal bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, diagnosed with a technetium pertechnetate scan. Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency in school-aged children: periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, fever and rebound; ultrasound is first-line imaging in children, to limit radiation.

Acute gastroenteritis is usually viral (rotavirus before vaccination, now norovirus predominates). Management rests on assessing the degree of dehydration (capillary refill, mucous membranes, skin turgor, tachycardia) and replacing losses, with oral rehydration solution the first-line treatment even in many moderately dehydrated children. Antiemetics such as ondansetron can facilitate oral rehydration; antimotility agents are avoided. Antibiotics are not indicated for most cases and may worsen Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli infection, which can lead to haemolytic uremic syndrome. Isotonic fluid is used for intravenous resuscitation. Bloody diarrhoea, fever and a recent undercooked beef history raise the possibility of this organism.

Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DQ2 and DQ8), with villous atrophy in the small intestine. Presentation ranges from diarrhoea, bloating and failure to thrive to iron deficiency anaemia, short stature, delayed puberty or dermatitis herpetiformis. Screening uses IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with a total IgA level, as IgA deficiency gives false negatives, and confirmation uses biopsy while the child is eating gluten. Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Functional constipation, the commonest cause of chronic abdominal pain and soiling, is managed with disimpaction, osmotic laxatives and toileting behaviour, after organic causes such as Hirschsprung disease have been considered in infants.

lessons.title: Congenital and Acquired Heart Disease
body: Congenital heart disease affects about 1 percent of live births and is the commonest category of birth defect. The physiologic logic is the direction and consequence of shunting. Left-to-right shunts (acyanotic) increase pulmonary blood flow, and over years can cause pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome with shunt reversal and cyanosis. Cyanotic lesions send deoxygenated blood to the systemic circulation, and obstruction lesions cause pressure overload.

Ventricular septal defect is the most common lesion. A small defect produces a loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and little shunt; a large defect causes heart failure at 1 to 2 months as pulmonary resistance falls, with poor feeding, sweating and tachypnoea. Many small defects close spontaneously. Atrial septal defect gives a fixed split second heart sound and a soft systolic ejection murmur from increased flow across the pulmonary valve, with often late presentation. Patent ductus arteriosus gives a continuous machinery murmur, and is common in preterm infants. Indomethacin or ibuprofen closes the ductus by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, whereas prostaglandin E1 keeps it open in ductal-dependent lesions. Atrioventricular septal defect is associated with Down syndrome.

Cyanotic lesions are remembered as the five Ts: tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia and total anomalous pulmonary venous return. Tetralogy of Fallot comprises a large ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow obstruction, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of obstruction determines cyanosis. Cyanotic tet spells occur in toddlers who squat, which increases systemic vascular resistance and decreases the right-to-left shunt, and the chest radiograph shows a boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary markings. Transposition of the great arteries causes severe cyanosis in the first day or two in a well-grown infant; a narrow mediastinum gives an egg-on-a-string appearance, and survival depends on mixing through a patent foramen ovale or ductus, so prostaglandin E1 and balloon atrial septostomy are used before an arterial switch operation. It is more frequent in infants of diabetic mothers.

Coarctation of the aorta, near the ductus insertion, causes upper-extremity hypertension, weak or delayed femoral pulses, and a radial-femoral delay, and in severe neonatal cases shock when the ductus closes. Rib notching appears in older children. It is associated with Turner syndrome and bicuspid aortic valve. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome presents with shock at ductal closure, and is another ductal-dependent lesion.

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis in children younger than 5 years. Diagnosis rests on fever for 5 or more days plus 4 of 5 features: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked red lips), polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy (usually unilateral and at least 1.5 cm) and extremity changes (oedema, later periungual desquamation). Coronary artery aneurysm is the feared complication, so echocardiography is done early. Intravenous immunoglobulin within the first 10 days, with aspirin, reduces aneurysm risk. The AHA 2024 update kept the diagnostic criteria unchanged, defined high risk as age 6 months or younger or a coronary z-score of 2.5 or more, and supports adding a second agent such as a corticosteroid or infliximab to intravenous immunoglobulin for high-risk patients, with closer early echocardiographic follow-up. Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis, diagnosed by the Jones criteria with migratory arthritis, carditis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. Chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis is the late consequence. Secondary prophylaxis with penicillin prevents recurrence.

lessons.title: Pediatric Endocrinology
body: Pediatric endocrinology revolves around two themes: hormone deficiency or excess and the timing of growth and puberty. Disorders in children often arise from autoimmunity or from inherited enzyme defects.

Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, with autoantibodies to insulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, islet antigen-2 and zinc transporter 8 and an association with HLA-DR3 and DR4. The classic presentation is polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and sometimes secondary enuresis in a thin child, and about a third present in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Without insulin, hepatic glucose output rises, lipolysis feeds ketone production, osmotic diuresis depletes volume and potassium, and the acidosis produces Kussmaul respiration and a fruity breath. Total body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium is normal or high at presentation because acidosis shifts potassium out of cells, so potassium must be monitored and replaced once urine output is established. Treatment is isotonic fluid resuscitation given with care and continuous insulin infusion with frequent monitoring (ISPAD 2022). Cerebral oedema is the most feared complication, occurring in the first 24 hours and signalled by headache, bradycardia, hypertension and altered consciousness; avoid aggressive fluid boluses and overly rapid osmolality changes. Long-term care includes insulin regimens, glucose monitoring, screening for thyroid disease and celiac disease, and later retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.

Congenital hypothyroidism is detected on newborn screening, as signs are subtle early: prolonged jaundice, constipation, a large tongue, umbilical hernia, hypotonia and a hoarse cry. Most cases in iodine-sufficient regions are thyroid dysgenesis. Thyroid hormone is essential for brain development in the first years, and prompt levothyroxine prevents intellectual disability. Acquired hypothyroidism in older children is usually Hashimoto thyroiditis, with growth failure but also, characteristically, delayed bone age and often weight gain.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency, an autosomal recessive defect that blocks cortisol and aldosterone synthesis and drives androgen excess through high ACTH. Females with the classic form have virilised (ambiguous) genitalia at birth; males appear normal. Salt wasting causes vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock at 1 to 2 weeks. Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone confirms the diagnosis, and treatment replaces glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid. Newborn screening detects it.

Growth and puberty. Short stature is evaluated by growth velocity, parental heights and bone age. Familial short stature has normal velocity and a normal bone age, constitutional delay has a delayed bone age with later catch-up and a family history of late puberty, and a pathologic cause such as growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, Turner syndrome, celiac disease or chronic illness shows slow velocity. Precocious puberty is the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls and 9 in boys. Most cases in girls are idiopathic central precocity, while boys more often have a pathologic cause such as a CNS lesion, so imaging is considered. Central precocious puberty is treated with a GnRH agonist. Peripheral causes include adrenal and gonadal tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Premature thelarche and adrenarche are benign variants without rapid progression. Delayed puberty is no breast development by 13 in girls or no testicular enlargement by 14 in boys.

lessons.title: Pediatric Neurology
body: Neurologic diagnosis in children begins with localisation and timing: acute or chronic, static or progressive, focal or generalised. Because the brain is still developing, a static insult yields a changing picture as the child grows, whereas loss of acquired skills indicates a progressive condition.

Febrile seizures occur between 6 months and 5 years in a febrile child without intracranial infection or a known seizure disorder. Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes and do not recur within 24 hours. Complex seizures are focal, prolonged or recurrent in the same illness. The AAP 2011 guideline states that after a simple febrile seizure in a well-appearing child, neuroimaging, EEG and routine labs are not needed; lumbar puncture is needed when meningeal signs are present, and is an option in infants of 6 to 12 months whose Haemophilus influenzae type b or pneumococcal immunization is deficient or unknown, or who have been pretreated with antibiotics. Age under 12 months alone is no longer the criterion; that came from the older 1996 guideline. Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence, and continuous antiseizure drugs are not recommended. The risk of later epilepsy is only slightly above the general population for simple febrile seizures.

Epilepsy is recurrent unprovoked seizures. Absence epilepsy begins at 4 to 10 years with brief staring spells without a postictal state, provoked by hyperventilation, and the EEG shows 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Ethosuximide is the classic drug of choice for absence seizures alone. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy presents in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks, generalised tonic-clonic seizures and absences, triggered by sleep deprivation, and is treated with a broad-spectrum agent. Infantile spasms (West syndrome) occur at 3 to 8 months as clusters of flexor spasms with developmental regression, and the EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. They are an emergency of brain development, and common causes include tuberous sclerosis; first-line treatments are ACTH or corticosteroids, and vigabatrin especially in tuberous sclerosis. Benign rolandic epilepsy causes nocturnal facial twitching in school-aged children with normal development and usually resolves in adolescence. Status epilepticus is treated first with a benzodiazepine. New-onset seizures prompt a search for a cause, from hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance to infection and trauma, including abusive head trauma in infants.

Cerebral palsy is a group of nonprogressive disorders of movement and posture from injury to the developing brain in the perinatal period or early infancy. Risk factors include prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, intraventricular haemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, kernicterus and congenital infection. Spastic types are the most common, with diplegia, hemiplegia and quadriplegia patterns, and persistent primitive reflexes and early hand preference before 12 months should raise concern. Care is multidisciplinary: therapy, spasticity management, orthopaedics and attention to associated epilepsy, vision, feeding and cognition. Cognition may be normal.

Headache in children is common and mostly benign, with migraine and tension types the main primary headaches. Red flags for a mass lesion or raised intracranial pressure include morning headache with vomiting, worsening pattern, nocturnal awakening, neurologic deficit, papilloedema, a headache in a child younger than 3 and a change in personality. Posterior fossa tumours such as medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma and ependymoma are the commonest paediatric brain tumours and cause ataxia and obstructive hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus in infants shows rapid head growth, a tense fontanelle and the sunsetting eye sign.

Neurocutaneous syndromes: neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas, optic glioma, autosomal dominant on chromosome 17), tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches, facial angiofibromas, seizures, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas) and Sturge-Weber syndrome (a port-wine stain in the V1 distribution with leptomeningeal angioma and seizures).

lessons.title: Pediatric Hematology and Oncology
body: The first step in the child with anaemia is the mean corpuscular volume and the reticulocyte count. Microcytic anaemia in childhood is most often iron deficiency, from inadequate intake (excess cow milk in toddlers, which also causes occult gut blood loss), rapid growth and, in adolescents, menstrual loss. Lead poisoning, thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease are alternatives. A normal ferritin, a low MCV and a normal or high red cell count favour thalassaemia trait. Treatment of iron deficiency is oral iron and diet, then recheck of the haemoglobin and reticulocyte response. Screening for anaemia is recommended at about 12 months.

Sickle cell disease is a recessive disorder of the beta-globin gene (Glu6Val) in which deoxygenated haemoglobin S polymerises, sickling red cells, causing haemolysis and vaso-occlusion. Fetal haemoglobin protects infants for the first months. Manifestations: dactylitis in infancy, vaso-occlusive pain crises, acute chest syndrome (the leading cause of death), splenic sequestration in young children, aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19, stroke and, because functional asplenia develops early, risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms. Newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis in early childhood, up-to-date pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination, transcranial Doppler screening for stroke risk, and hydroxyurea (which raises fetal haemoglobin) are central to care, and fever in a child with sickle cell disease is an emergency needing prompt cultures and antibiotics.

Bleeding disorders. Hemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX) are X-linked recessive, producing deep bleeding into joints and muscles, bleeding after circumcision, with prolonged PTT and normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time; treatment is factor replacement and emicizumab for hemophilia A. Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, causes mucocutaneous bleeding with epistaxis and menorrhagia, with prolonged bleeding time and sometimes a prolonged PTT. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) typically follows a viral illness in a well child, producing petechiae and bruising with isolated thrombocytopenia and a normal examination apart from the skin. Most children recover spontaneously, and intravenous immunoglobulin or steroids are used for bleeding or very low counts; a child with ITP who has anaemia, abnormal white cells, lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly needs evaluation for leukaemia. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) shows palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis with a normal platelet count. Haemolytic uremic syndrome is covered under gastroenteritis.

Childhood cancer is rare but is the leading disease-related cause of death in children in many countries. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the most common, peaking at 2 to 5 years, with fatigue, fever, bone pain, pallor, bruising, hepatosplenomegaly and an abnormal blood count. Down syndrome and prior chemotherapy are risk factors. Diagnosis is by bone marrow examination, and prognosis in children is generally excellent with modern risk-adapted protocols. Tumour lysis syndrome is a risk with chemotherapy. Brain tumours are the most common solid tumours. Neuroblastoma, from neural crest cells of the sympathetic chain or adrenal medulla, presents in toddlers with an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, opsoclonus-myoclonus, periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes) and raised urinary catecholamine metabolites; MYCN amplification predicts poor prognosis. Wilms tumour presents in children aged 2 to 5 as a smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline, often with haematuria and hypertension, and is associated with WAGR syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and aniridia. Retinoblastoma presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and an RB1 mutation; heritable disease has increased risk of second cancers. Lymphomas and osteosarcoma (with bone pain and a sunburst pattern around the knee) and Ewing sarcoma (onion skin periosteal reaction in the diaphysis) complete the common list.

lessons.title: Recognising Child Abuse and Neglect
body: Child maltreatment includes physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse and neglect, and neglect is the most common type. Clinicians are in a unique position to recognise it, and missed cases carry a risk of repeated and sometimes fatal injury. The method is to ask whether the injury is consistent with the history and with the child's developmental ability, and to avoid deciding on the basis of the caregiver's demeanour or social background. Bias in both directions causes harm: wealthy families are less likely to be suspected and poor or minority families more likely to be wrongly suspected, so a structured approach helps.

Red flags in the history are a delay in seeking care, a story that changes or is inconsistent with the injury, an injury that does not match the child's developmental stage (a non-mobile infant with a fracture or bruise), an explanation of unwitnessed trauma, and blaming a sibling. Bruising is the commonest sign. Patterns that raise concern are bruises in an infant who is not yet cruising, bruises on the torso, ears, neck, frenulum, angle of the jaw or buttocks (the TEN-4-FACESp rule flags bruising of the torso, ear or neck in a child under 4 years, and any bruising in an infant under 4 months), patterned marks such as a looped cord or hand print, and bruises in multiple stages. Ordinary childhood bruises sit over bony prominences such as shins and forehead. Burns that show immersion with a stocking or glove pattern, sparing of flexed creases, sharp demarcation and symmetry suggest forced immersion; cigarette burns are round and uniform.

Fractures that are highly specific for abuse include classic metaphyseal lesions (corner or bucket-handle fractures), posterior rib fractures, scapular, sternal and spinous process fractures, and multiple fractures of different ages. Femur fractures in a non-ambulatory child warrant concern. A skeletal survey is recommended for suspected physical abuse in children younger than 2 years. Accidental causes and medical mimics such as osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets, and bleeding disorders must be considered and excluded when appropriate, though mimics are less common than abuse among suspicious presentations.

Abusive head trauma is the leading cause of death from child abuse in infants. Violent shaking, with or without impact, tears bridging veins and causes subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages (extensive, multilayered and extending to the periphery) and hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, often with no external signs. Presentations are vague: irritability, vomiting, poor feeding, apnoea or seizures. Evaluation requires neuroimaging, dilated retinal examination and skeletal survey. Short falls from household furniture rarely cause serious intracranial injury. Sexual abuse presentations include disclosure, behavioural changes, sexually transmitted infection or pregnancy, and a normal genital examination is common and does not exclude abuse; this evaluation is done with specialised child abuse teams and trained forensic interviewers.

Clinicians are mandated reporters in all US states: the legal threshold is reasonable suspicion, not certainty or proof. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on state reporting systems, while state laws set details. Reports go to child protective services or law enforcement, and good-faith reporters have immunity. The clinician does not investigate, accuse or confront, but documents objectively using the child's own words in quotation marks, photographs, injuries and the caregiver's account, and ensures the child's safety, which may mean admission. Munchausen syndrome by proxy (now called factitious disorder imposed on another) involves a caregiver who falsifies or induces illness in a child. Neglect covers failure to meet physical, medical, educational or emotional needs, and can present as failure to thrive, poor hygiene and missed care. Prevention counsels about safe sleep, abusive-head-trauma education (crying plans for infants) and positive parenting, and screens for risk such as intimate partner violence and parental depression.

A worked example: a 5-month-old is brought with a swollen thigh after the father says he rolled off the sofa. Radiographs show a femoral shaft fracture and the survey reveals healing posterior rib fractures. A fracture in a non-ambulatory infant with an inconsistent story and multiple fractures of different ages warrants a report to child protective services and a safe disposition.

lessons.title: Adolescent Medicine
body: Adolescence brings rapid physical change, identity formation, risk-taking and growing independence. The leading causes of death in teenagers are accidents (unintentional injuries, including motor vehicle crashes), then homicide and suicide in recent CDC data for ages 15 to 19, so the burden is mostly behavioural and preventable. The adolescent visit therefore centres on development, safety and counselling more than on disease.

Confidential care is the foundation. Teenagers are more likely to disclose and seek care when they trust that private information will stay private. Part of every visit is seen with the adolescent alone. Confidentiality has limits that the clinician explains at the start: risk of serious harm to self or others and abuse. In the US, minors can consent on their own to certain services, such as contraception, sexually transmitted infection testing and treatment and often mental health and substance-use care, but laws differ by state, so clinicians must know their jurisdiction. The HEADSS or HEEADSSS interview (home, education and employment, eating, activities, drugs, sexuality, suicide and depression, safety) is a structured psychosocial history. Bright Futures offers the periodic schedule, and the AAP recommends confidential screening.

Puberty is staged using the Tanner (sexual maturity rating) system. In girls the sequence is breast budding (thelarche), then pubic hair, peak height velocity and menarche, roughly two years after thelarche. In boys, testicular enlargement is the first sign, and peak height velocity comes late. Gynaecomastia is common and transient in pubertal boys. Idiopathic scoliosis is screened for through forward bending, and sports participation evaluations focus on cardiac history such as syncope with exertion and a family history of sudden death, which suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or long QT syndrome.

Eating disorders usually start in adolescence. Anorexia nervosa features restriction of intake, intense fear of gaining weight and disturbed body image; complications include bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, amenorrhoea, osteopenia, electrolyte disturbance and, in the restricting type, risk of sudden death. Bulimia nervosa involves binge eating with compensatory behaviours such as vomiting, which causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, dental erosion, parotid enlargement and Russell sign. Family-based treatment is first-line for adolescent anorexia. Refeeding syndrome, with hypophosphataemia, is a risk during initial nutritional rehabilitation, and indications for admission include instability and severe malnutrition. The female athlete triad refers to low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone density.

Depression affects a considerable proportion of teenagers. The USPSTF (2022) recommends screening for major depressive disorder in adolescents 12 to 18 years of age, with systems in place for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. Suicide risk is asked about directly, and doing so does not plant the idea. Treatments are psychotherapy (cognitive behavioural therapy, interpersonal therapy), and for moderate to severe depression, an SSRI such as fluoxetine, alongside close monitoring for suicidal thinking early in treatment because of the boxed warning for people younger than 25. Substance use screening asks about alcohol, cannabis, nicotine and vaping, and other drugs, using brief tools such as CRAFFT, with a brief intervention for risk. Sexual health care covers abstinence, condom use, contraception including long-acting reversible methods, HPV vaccination and screening for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in sexually active females under 25, with HIV testing. Cervical screening begins at 21 and is not needed earlier in healthy adolescents.

A worked example: a 16-year-old girl is seen for a sports physical. Alone, she says she is sexually active, does not use contraception and has had vaginal discharge. The right approach is confidential counselling, urine nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, offering contraception and a pregnancy test, and treating her partner appropriately, while respecting her right to confidential care under state law.

lessons.title: Developmental and Behavioural Disorders
body: Developmental and behavioural problems are among the most common reasons for a pediatric visit, and the clinician must tell variants of normal from disorders that benefit from early intervention. Three principles apply: use validated screening, look for the contribution of hearing, vision, sleep and family stress, and refer early since early intervention improves outcome.

Autism spectrum disorder is defined (DSM-5-TR) by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, with symptoms present in early development and causing impairment. Early signs include no response to name, poor eye contact, absence of pointing and shared attention by 12 to 14 months, language delay, loss of previously acquired language, and repetitive movements or insistence on sameness. Autism-specific screening with the M-CHAT-R/F is recommended at 18 and 24 months (AAP). Diagnosis follows comprehensive developmental evaluation, hearing testing and often genetic testing such as chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing. Behavioural and educational approaches, such as applied behavioural analysis and speech and occupational therapy, are first-line; medication such as risperidone or aripiprazole targets severe irritability and aggression and not the core features. Large epidemiologic studies have found no causal association with vaccines, and the dramatic increase in diagnoses reflects broader criteria and better detection plus some true risk factors, such as older parental age.

ADHD is a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity across settings, starting before age 12. The AAP 2019 guideline addresses children 4 to 18 years, and recommends evidence-based parent training for preschoolers (4 to 5 years) as first-line, with methylphenidate as an option when behavioural interventions fail. For school-aged children (6 to 11) and adolescents, medication together with behavioural therapy is recommended. Stimulants (methylphenidate and amphetamine) block dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake or promote release, and adverse effects include decreased appetite, insomnia, tics and, rarely, cardiovascular effects, so a history of syncope or family history of sudden death is obtained. Non-stimulants such as atomoxetine and the alpha-2 agonist guanfacine are alternatives. Diagnosis needs a rating scale from more than one setting, with attention to conditions that mimic or coexist with ADHD, such as anxiety, learning disability, sleep disorders, hearing problems and trauma.

Specific learning disorders (reading, written expression, mathematics) and language disorders are identified by evaluation at school and by speech-language pathologists, and Individuals with Disabilities Education Act services provide individualised education plans. Speech delay with a normal hearing test and normal social engagement is often an isolated expressive language disorder.

Enuresis is intermittent urinary incontinence during sleep after age 5. Primary enuresis, never dry for 6 months, is the most common, and is familial, associated with delayed bladder maturation, nocturnal polyuria and deep sleep. Evaluation is a history and urinalysis to look for diabetes, infection or constipation, and treatment includes reassurance, motivation, an enuresis alarm (the most effective for long-term cure) and desmopressin for situations such as sleepovers. Secondary enuresis after a dry period raises concern about stress, infection, diabetes or abuse. Encopresis is stool soiling usually from constipation with overflow. Temper tantrums, breath-holding spells, sleep problems and picky eating are common in toddlers and respond to consistent routines, and breath-holding spells are benign but should be differentiated from seizures and from iron deficiency, which can worsen them.

questions.prompt: From which age are the WHO growth standards, rather than the CDC charts, recommended for monitoring a child's growth in the United States?
choices: From birth to 2 years of age
From 2 years until puberty, because they include body mass index references for older children
From birth until the end of adolescence, because they replace all national growth charts in use
From 6 months until 5 years, because that is when complementary foods change the pattern

questions.prompt: A 2-year-old boy has no words, does not point and does not turn to his name. He had said a few words at 15 months. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Brain MRI and genetic panel as the first step before any developmental referral
Audiology plus developmental referral
Reassurance that language develops later in boys, with a repeat visit at the 3-year check
A trial of speech practice at home and a follow-up visit after six more months

questions.prompt: A 14-month-old girl has been healthy. She cruises but does not walk alone, babbles, uses two words with meaning, waves and points. Her growth is along the 40th percentile. Which statement best describes her?
choices: Global developmental delay, because she has fewer than five words at this age
Early autism spectrum disorder, because she does not yet walk without holding on
Normal variation in walking age
Gross motor delay, because walking should be established by 12 months in all children

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old has weight dropping from the 50th to the 10th percentile over three months, while length and head circumference remain near the 50th. Which cause is most likely?
choices: A genetic growth disorder, which affects weight and length together from the first weeks
Growth hormone deficiency, which causes marked weight loss with preserved length
Hydrocephalus, which causes weight faltering through raised intracranial pressure
Inadequate caloric intake

questions.prompt: At a 9-month visit, a mother's score on a parent-completed screening questionnaire is below the cutoff in the communication and fine motor domains. The infant is otherwise well. What should the clinician do?
choices: Refer for evaluation and early intervention now
Repeat the screen at the 12-month visit and refer only if the score is still below the cutoff
Order a karyotype and thyroid studies and refer only if these are abnormal
Advise increased play time and review the child at 18 months with the autism screen
